Pool Pump Repair in Yuma

A pump that hums, screeches, drips or keeps shutting off stops the whole pool from filtering. Call the free line any hour and you are put through to an independent, locally owned Yuma-area pool company that can look at it in person.

Pool pump repair in Yuma usually starts with a sound or a puddle. The pump draws water in at the skimmer and at the drain on the pool floor, forces it through the filter, then returns it to the pool through the wall jets. Everything else depends on that flow: the chlorine gets mixed in, the filter catches dust, and an automatic cleaner can move. When the pump stops, or runs but moves less water, the pool starts to slip within days in hot weather.

Below: the common symptoms, the checks that are safe to make, the parts that wear, published costs, and running a pump on Yuma electricity. Problems with filters, heaters and salt cells are covered on the pool equipment repair page, and cracks, leaks and other structural work on the pool repair page.

Yuma Pool Cleaning Pro does not fix pumps. It is a free phone line. An automated assistant answers (928) 615-5224, asks what the pump is doing, and puts you through to an independent, locally owned company in the area that works on pools. That company inspects the pump, gives its own quote and bills you directly.

Pump symptoms and what they usually point to

A pump tends to warn you before it quits. The table below matches the signs people notice most with the causes that published repair guides link them to, the safe check you can make, and the point where it becomes a job for a pool technician.

Common pool pump symptoms, likely causes, safe homeowner checks and when to call
What you noticeCommon causesSafe checkCall a pro when
Humming, but nothing spinsA failed start capacitor or a jammed motor or impellerSwitch the pump off at the timer. Look for a basket packed with leaves or debris.It still hums after the baskets are clear. Do not keep restarting it.
Screeching or grindingWorn motor bearings, often after years of use or after running dryMake sure the pump is full of water and the baskets are clear.The noise continues. Bearings and motors are repair work.
Water dripping under the pumpA worn shaft seal or a tired O-ring at a fittingLook for the drip and note where it starts. Keep the area around the motor dry.Water is near the motor or the drip keeps growing.
Air in the lid, weak flow, losing primeAir getting into the suction side through a loose fitting or cracked O-ring, low water, or clogged basketsCheck the water level at the skimmer, empty both baskets, and look at the lid O-ring for cracks.The lid stays full of air with the water level and baskets right.
Shuts off, then restarts laterOverheating from a blocked motor vent, debris in the pump or a hard-working motorClear leaves and gravel away from the motor vents and empty the baskets.It keeps cycling or feels very hot to the touch.
Trips the breaker or GFCIAn electrical fault in the motor, wiring or circuitReset the breaker or GFCI once.It trips again. Leave it off and call. This is electrical work.

Checks that are safe to make

  • Turn the pump off before you open anything, then empty both baskets, the one in the skimmer and the one at the front of the pump.
  • Look at the water level. When the water line drops to the lower half of the skimmer opening, air can get drawn in.
  • Look at the pump lid O-ring. A flattened, cracked or dry ring lets air in.
  • Confirm the timer or automation schedule has not shifted after a power outage.
  • Reset a tripped breaker or GFCI one time only.
  • Clear leaves, gravel and dust away from the motor so it can breathe.

Anything beyond that, such as opening the motor, touching the capacitor or changing wiring, should stay with a professional. Never run a pump dry for long to "test" it.

Repair the pump or replace it

A pool pump has a handful of parts that wear: the lid and its O-ring, the strainer basket, the impeller that moves the water, the shaft seal that keeps water away from the motor, the motor bearings, and on many single speed motors a start capacitor. Most of these can be replaced on their own. The question is whether the rest of the pump is worth keeping.

A repair often makes sense when

  • The pump is well inside its expected life, which Angi estimates at roughly 8 to 15 years.
  • The trouble is one worn part, such as a seal, an O-ring or a set of bearings.
  • The housing is sound, with no cracks.
  • The repair costs well under half the price of a new pump.

A replacement is worth pricing when

  • The repair would pass about half the cost of a new pump, the point Angi uses as a rule of thumb.
  • The motor or the housing is badly damaged.
  • The same pump keeps failing.
  • It is an older single speed pump and you want lower power bills.

The federal rule on new pump motors

Energy standards from the U.S. Department of Energy changed which motors factories can make. For motors rated 1.15 to 5 total horsepower and built from September 29, 2025 onward, variable speed control is required. Small motors, those from 0.5 up to 1.15 total horsepower, come under the rule later, on September 28, 2027. Then in April 2026 the DOE said it would hold off on enforcing that requirement for small motors built before March 26, 2029. Nothing in the rule forces you to remove equipment that works. It matters when a motor fails, because the replacement may have to be a variable speed model.

Running a pool pump in Yuma heat and on APS time-of-use hours

How long a pump should run is one of the most common questions, and there is no single correct answer. The idea behind it is turnover: moving the full volume of pool water through the filter. How many hours that takes depends on the size of the pool and how fast the pump moves water. A variable speed pump set to a low speed runs longer to move the same water, yet the U.S. Department of Energy's Building America guide shows it can use less energy overall. ENERGY STAR notes that a pump at half speed uses about one eighth of the energy. The Arizona Department of Water Resources also recommends limiting pump run time to save energy. A pool technician can set a schedule that keeps your water clear without wasting power.

  • APS on-peak hoursOn current APS time-of-use plans, on-peak is 4 to 7 p.m. on weekdays all year, and some older plans use 3 to 8 p.m. APS recommends running the pool pump off-peak.
  • Winter super off-peakFrom November through April, APS bills include a super off-peak period from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. on weekdays. APS says running the pool pump in that window could save up to $120 a year.
  • Not on APS?In Wellton, the Wellton-Mohawk Irrigation and Drainage District provides electricity. In the Foothills and Gadsden, your electric bill names your provider. Ask that provider about its rates.
  • Heat on the equipment padNWS normals give Yuma about 118 days a year when the high reaches 100 degrees or more, usually from late April into early October, with about 25 days at 110 or above. A motor already straining against a clogged basket has a hard time on those afternoons, so keep its vents clear.
  • Dust in the basketsA NOAA weather service memo finds the most blowing dust reports in Arizona's low desert, which includes Yuma, with reports rising sharply in July. After a storm, empty the skimmer and pump baskets so the pump does not starve for water.

If you spend the summer away from Yuma, a pump problem can go unnoticed for weeks. Ask whoever services the pool to tell you if the pump stops. For the year-round routine, see the Yuma pool maintenance schedule.

Who is allowed to work on a pool pump in Arizona

The state license for home pool service and minor repair work is the R-6, whose full name is Residential Swimming Pool Service and Repair. The Arizona Registrar of Contractors issues it. R-6 excludes electrical work beyond the first disconnect and gas lines, so a new circuit or rewiring belongs with a licensed electrical contractor. A careful pool technician will tell you when part of the job needs someone else.

  1. Describe the symptom. Say what you hear or see and when it started. The table above gives you the words.
  2. Let the company inspect. A technician checks flow, the seal, the motor and the electrical supply before naming a cause.
  3. Get the options in writing. Ask for the repair price and, if relevant, a replacement price.
  4. Check the license. Request the company's ROC license number and search it yourself.

Check the contractor license. Arizona's Registrar of Contractors (ROC) issues the licenses for pool work. Residential R-6, Swimming Pool Service and Repair, is the classification for servicing a home pool and handling minor repairs. Building a new pool or putting in a whole new plaster or pebble surface falls under construction classifications such as B-5. Routine cleaning on its own is a gray area the ROC has not written a clear rule on, so simply ask the company what it holds. Then type its ROC number into the ROC contractor search (new tab) to see if the license is current, what type it is and any recent complaints. Yuma Pool Cleaning Pro does not run this lookup for you.

Common questions

How often do pool pumps need to be replaced?

It depends on the pump. Angi's estimate for a typical pool pump is roughly 8 to 15 years, and the size, the pump type and the upkeep all move that number. Many pumps need a seal, bearings or a motor along the way and keep going. A pump is usually replaced when a repair would cost a large share of a new pump, when the housing is cracked, or when it keeps failing.

How often does my pool pump need to run?

Published sources do not give one number of hours that fits every pool. The goal is to move all of the pool water through the filter often enough to keep it clear, which depends on the pool size, the pump, the filter and how much dust and debris land in the water. ENERGY STAR notes that cutting run time from 24 hours to 6 hours a day cuts the energy used by 75 percent, and that a pump at half speed uses about one eighth of the energy. Ask the pool company to set a schedule for your pool, and on an APS time-of-use plan keep it out of the 4 to 7 p.m. weekday on-peak window.

Why is my pool pump humming but not pumping?

A hum with no spinning often points to a failed start capacitor or something jamming the motor or impeller, according to Angi. Shut the pump off at the timer and avoid restarting it again and again, since a motor that cannot turn heats up. The capacitor and motor are electrical parts, so leave the covers on and have a pool technician or electrician look at it.

How much does pool pump repair cost?

In Angi's 2026 figures, most pump repairs fall between $100 and $700, and many land near $350. Angi lists $100 to $250 for a new shaft seal and $350 to $700 to swap the whole motor. For a complete new pump with installation, Angi's national average is about $1,300. All of these are national numbers in print, not a price from this line. A Yuma company gives its own quote once it has seen the pump, and real quotes vary.

Do I have to buy a variable speed pool pump now?

A federal efficiency rule from the U.S. Department of Energy requires variable speed on motors rated 1.15 to 5 total horsepower when they are built from September 29, 2025 onward. Smaller motors follow later. The rule is about what factories can make, so a pump that runs fine today can stay where it is. If yours fails, the replacement motor on the shelf may already be variable speed.
